findings.committee: Portfolio Holder for Corporate and Finance
findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Position for 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA balances declining year-on-year despite operational surplus; capital needs outpacing internal generation
findings.detail: HRA balances fell from £3.949m to £3.827m in 2025/26 despite the account running an operational surplus. The surplus was wholly applied to fund the HRA capital programme in line with the 30-year business plan, meaning the council is drawing down reserves rather than building them.
findings.matters: Lenders assess long-term HRA sustainability and financing assumptions; if this pattern continues, the HRA will face pressure to borrow at scale or raise rents significantly to fund capital needs, both carrying financial and political risk.
findings.figures: HRA opening balances £3.949m, closing balances £3.827m (£122k decrease)
findings.quote: As a result of the surplus position, Housing Revenue Account Balances increased. However, these balances have then been used to fund the HRA capital programme, in line with the 30-year HRA Business Plan, which has meant that balances have decreased at the end of the financial year.

findings.committee: Portfolio Holder for Corporate and Finance
findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Position for 2025/26
findings.headline: General Fund reserves stand at only £25k above the council's approved minimum level—virtually no buffer
findings.detail: General Fund balances at 31 March 2026 were £2.125m, just £25,000 above the minimum level the council has approved for prudent financial management. This leaves minimal headroom.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a key resilience indicator; balances at or near minimum level mean the council has little flexibility to absorb unexpected costs, income shortfalls, or emergencies without cutting services or seeking new borrowing.
findings.figures: General Fund balances £2.125m; approved minimum £2.100m
findings.quote: At the 31 March 2026, General Fund Balances stood at £2.125m which is £25,000 above the minimum level of balances the Council approved as part of the budget setting process.

findings.committee: Portfolio Holder for Corporate and Finance
findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Position for 2025/26
findings.headline: Major capital schemes experiencing slippage due to complex delivery issues, supply chain problems, and cost escalation
findings.detail: The council's capital programme faced slippage in 2025/26. Delays were caused by complex issues that must be resolved before main works proceed, supply chain disruption, and cost increases on schemes. Carry-forwards to 2026/27 are required.
findings.matters: Scheme delays signal delivery and governance risk; cost escalation increases borrowing requirements and impacts the balance sheet; lenders need to understand whether capital plans are realistic.
findings.figures: Approved capital programme 2025/26 of £78.837m; specific slippage amounts in Appendices 3–6
findings.quote: There has been slippage on the programme due to delays in large capital schemes due to complex issues having to be addressed before the main works can be completed, supply chain issues and increased costs.

findings.committee: Portfolio Holder for Corporate and Finance
findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Position for 2025/26
findings.headline: Recruitment difficulties forcing use of expensive agency staff rather than direct employment
findings.detail: The council faces staffing recruitment challenges common to local authorities. Rather than leave posts vacant, numerous roles are being filled via agency staff arrangements at significantly higher cost than direct employment.
findings.matters: This represents an ongoing structural cost pressure reducing budget flexibility; if the council cannot reduce agency spend, it crowds out other priorities and erodes surplus positions.
findings.figures: Specific agency cost not quantified; pay award saving was £147k General Fund and £67k HRA
findings.quote: There are a number of vacant posts throughout the authority and in order to ensure that key services continue to be delivered, some roles have been covered through agency staff, which is more expensive than employing staff directly.

findings.committee: Portfolio Holder for Corporate and Finance
findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Position for 2025/26
findings.headline: Council heavily dependent on commercial/industrial rent income which is at risk from tenant cost pressures
findings.detail: Mansfield generates a high proportion of its income from commercial and industrial rents. The paper explicitly flags that businesses are experiencing the same pressures as the council—rising energy and staffing costs—and states the council is closely monitoring this income stream as a result.
findings.matters: Lenders assess revenue stability and diversification; heavy concentration in a pressure-sensitive income stream creates vulnerability to debt servicing capacity if tenant viability deteriorates.
findings.figures: Proportion of income from commercial/industrial rents not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: The Council generates a high proportion of its income from commercial/industrial rents. Given that business are experiencing the same pressures as Mansfield District Council, such as increased energy and staffing costs, the Council continues to monitor this income stream closely.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Audit Strategy Memorandum – 2025/26
findings.headline: £25 million in housing repairs contracts awarded outside procurement rules following whistleblowing investigation
findings.detail: The council's internal audit, triggered by whistleblower reports, found that housing repairs work was systematically allocated to external contractors without following proper Contract Procedure Rules or governance decision-making. The breach was council-wide in scale: £25 million in spending circumvented normal procurement controls. While the council has retrospectively approved these contracts and implemented corrective actions, the auditor confirmed this represents a significant weakness in governance and value-for-money arrangements.
findings.matters: Procurement breaches of this magnitude mean the council cannot demonstrate it achieved value for money at the time of purchase. Without competitive tendering, costs could be inflated and services lower quality. The discovery through whistleblowing rather than routine oversight suggests governance structures failed.
findings.figures: £25 million
findings.quote: The total value of contracts not procured in accordance with these rules was £25 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for External Audit Strategy Memorandum – 2025/26
findings.headline: Bank reconciliations were not performed for 19 months (April 2024 to November 2025) due to new finance system implementation and staffing constraints
findings.detail: A critical internal control broke down during the council's transition to a new finance system. Bank reconciliations—essential for catching errors and fraud—were not performed for nearly two years. The council attributed this to the system changeover combined with insufficient finance team capacity. The auditor classified this as a significant weakness in governance arrangements, meaning the council failed to gain proper assurance over the effectiveness of its internal controls.
findings.matters: A 19-month gap in bank reconciliations means potential errors, fraud, or misstatement could go undetected. This indicates systemic internal control failure, directly affecting the reliability of the council's financial records and management's ability to oversee spending.
findings.figures: 19 months (April 2024 to November 2025)
findings.quote: The Council confirmed that this lapse resulted from the implementation of a new finance system and associated procedural changes, combined with limited team capacity during this period.

findings.paper_title: INVESTMENT STRATEGY OUTTURN POSITION 2025/26
findings.headline: Debt restructuring is blocked by expensive PWLB early repayment premiums
findings.detail: The council cannot restructure or refinance its PWLB debt due to expensive early repayment premiums. No debt rescheduling was undertaken during 2025/26. This locks the council into its current debt profile regardless of market conditions.
findings.matters: If interest rates rise, the council has no option to reduce debt service costs through refinancing. This limits financial flexibility and increases vulnerability to rate shocks.
findings.figures: £54.673m PWLB debt with prohibitively expensive early repayment terms
findings.quote: The premium charge for early repayment of Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) debt remains relatively expensive for the loans in the Council's portfolio and therefore unattractive for debt rescheduling activity. No debt rescheduling has been undertaken during the period from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: INVESTMENT STRATEGY OUTTURN POSITION 2025/26
findings.headline: Borrowing increased by £29.5m to £85.8m in a single year
findings.detail: The council drew £39m in new loans during 2025/26, raising total borrowing from £56.3m to £85.8m—a 52% increase in gross debt. The portfolio comprises £54.7m PWLB debt, £31m borrowing from other local authorities, and £0.159m short-term Racecourse Trust borrowing.
findings.matters: A 52% increase in debt in one year materially raises future debt service costs. With interest rates volatile and inflation concerns rising, borrowing costs will likely increase further, compressing budget headroom.
findings.figures: £85.832m total borrowing (31 March 2026); increase of £29.506m; £39m new loans in year; £54.673m PWLB
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council held £85.832m loans (an increase of £29.506m on 31 March 2025). During the period 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026, £39m in new loans were taken out.

findings.paper_title: INVESTMENT STRATEGY OUTTURN POSITION 2025/26
findings.headline: Investment income fell by £1.17m year-on-year despite beating budget
findings.detail: Actual investment income in 2025/26 was £832,833.12 against a budget of £535,000, beating budget by £297,833. However, this represents a significant decline of £1,166,495.80 from prior year. The decline is driven by Bank Rate reductions from 4.50% to 3.75%, cutting average investment returns from 5.14% to 4.32%.
findings.matters: A £1.17m reduction in non-taxpayer revenue materially affects the council's financial flexibility and ability to fund discretionary activity. With rates now held at 3.75% and further cuts unlikely, this income stream will remain depressed.
findings.quote: The budget for investment income for 2025/26 was £535,000 compared against actual investment income achieved of £832,833.12, a decrease of £1,166,495.80 over the income in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: HRA debt-to-revenue ratio nearly quadrupling in four years
findings.detail: The HRA debt-to-revenue ratio rises from 1.22 in 2024/25 to 3.89 by 2028/29. The council is simultaneously increasing the HRA loan-to-value ratio from 14% to 44% of housing assets. This reflects a policy of significant new HRA borrowing for housing new build schemes and stock investment, with the debt burden increasing faster than rental income.
findings.matters: Debt-to-revenue ratios of nearly 4x indicate the HRA is becoming highly leveraged. HRA rents are regulated by government, limiting the council's ability to increase income to service growing debt. This severely constrains financial flexibility.
findings.quote: The ratio increases as the HRA debt level is expected to increase in order to deliver new build housing schemes and investment in the existing housing stock.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: Maintaining under-borrowed position creates refinancing risk if interest rates rise
findings.detail: The council has deliberately chosen not to borrow the full amount needed for capital expenditure, instead using cash reserves as a temporary measure. Strategy states this is prudent because 'medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed'. However, if rates do not fall as forecast, the council will be forced to borrow at higher rates to replenish depleted reserves. Current PWLB rates are 4.81% (5yr) to 6.01% (25yr).
findings.matters: This strategy is a bet on falling interest rates. If rates remain stable or rise, the council will face higher borrowing costs and will be forced to borrow into a potentially more expensive market when reserves run low.
findings.figures: PWLB certainty rates (22 Dec 2025): 5yr 4.81%, 10yr 5.39%, 25yr 6.01%, 50yr 5.78%; Under-borrowing position: £55.9m at start of period declining to £50.9m
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (CFR), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by tighter near-term monetary policy.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement growing faster than borrowing, funded by reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The CFR is forecast to grow from £117.9m to £253.7m by 2028/29, while external borrowing reaches only £202.9m. The gap (under-borrowing of £50.9m) is being filled by drawing down reserves and cash balances. Fund balances are forecast to fall from £50.7m to £29.0m. A £121.4m capital programme in 2026/27 alone is substantially above historical levels, including major HRA new build schemes.
findings.matters: Reserves are being consumed faster than income replaces them, reducing the council's cushion for adverse events. Once reserves are depleted, any shortfall in income or unexpected cost will require additional borrowing at potentially higher rates.
findings.figures: CFR: £117.925m (2024/25) → £253.737m (2028/29); External borrowing: £202.880m by 2028/29; Under-borrowing: £55.955m falling to £50.857m; Fund balances: £50.727m → £28.955m; Capital expenditure: £121.4m (2026/27)
findings.quote: Table 2 shows that the Council forecasts that borrowing will increase to £202.880Million (including maintaining a minimum £10million liquid funds) and so expects to comply with this recommendation during the next three years.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: HRA interest cover rate falling below peer average as debt grows
findings.detail: The Interest Cover Rate (how many times operating surplus covers interest costs) is forecast to fall from 3.83 in 2024/25 to 1.31 by 2028/29. The council notes that the average ICR for councils with an HRA is 2.24, meaning Mansfield will be below peer average from 2026/27 onwards and at the lower end of the peer range (1.20 to 4.50) by 2028/29. This occurs while HRA debt grows from £40.7m to £150.6m over the same period.
findings.matters: A declining interest cover rate suggests reduced financial resilience in the HRA to service its growing debt. This signals increasing financial stress in what is typically a council's most leveraged operation.
findings.quote: The average ICR for councils with an HRA was 2.24 when these indicators were introduced, with councils ranging between 1.20 to 4.50 therefore the Council is estimated to be above the average for 2025/26 but is expected to fall below the average in the future years.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: Loan-to-value on HRA housing stock forecast to reach 43–44% by 2027/28, within peer range but trending up sharply
findings.detail: HRA LTV rises from 14% (2024/25) to 44% (2028/29), approaching the regional average range of 35–48%. Driven by new-build and refurbishment financed by borrowing.
findings.matters: Confirms the HRA is now materially leveraged to its property asset base. At 44% LTV, loss of asset value or sharp decline in rental income would reduce equity. Regional peer comparisons suggest this is normal but the trajectory is steep and leaves little room for adverse events.
findings.quote: Loan To Value - calculates the level of debt (the HRA CFR) compared to the Value of the HRA assets. The regional average when these indicators were introduced for the East Midlands and Northern Regions is between the ranges of 35% to 48%.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: Council betting on falling interest rates via under-borrowed position of £50–56m
findings.detail: The council maintains external debt of £61m–£202m against a CFR of £117m–£253m, keeping £50–56m 'under-borrowed' (i.e., funded from reserves/working capital rather than loans). Strategy states this is 'prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall.' But the council acknowledges 'risks within the economic forecast' and wage growth still over 4.5%.
findings.matters: If interest rates do not fall as forecast, or if council needs cash urgently, it will be forced to borrow at rates higher than the current forecast 3.25%–3.5%. This is a material directional bet on monetary policy.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing forecast: 2025/26 £55.9m, 2026/27 £55.4m, 2027/28 £53.2m, 2028/29 £50.9m; Bank Rate forecast 3.75% (current) → 3.25% by Dec 2026
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (CFR), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels once prevailing inflation concerns are addressed by tighter near-term monetary policy.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio (£26m) financed entirely by external borrowing with discretionary MRP provision
findings.detail: The council holds approximately £26m in commercial property investments funded from external borrowing. Instead of conventional depreciation-based MRP, the council charges only a discretionary amount based on annual portfolio review and value trajectory. Initial gains are held in an earmarked volatility reserve. This policy defers principal repayment.
findings.matters: Non-standard MRP approach masks true principal repayment obligations and creates revenue flexibility that is contingent on property valuations holding. If property values decline or rents fall, the council has limited cushion and no systematic debt paydown.
findings.figures: Commercial property portfolio ~£26m funded by external borrowing; typical full 50-year MRP would charge £260k–£344k p.a. if 50% is land value; council charges discretionary amount based on annual review
findings.quote: Rather than charging a fixed amount each year, the Council believes that a prudent approach would be to review the value of the commercial property investments each year and then consider any requirement to set aside a prudent provision based on the value and expected trajectory of the holding.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: HRA debt-to-revenue ratio forecast to increase to 3.89 by 2028/29
findings.detail: The ratio of HRA debt to HRA gross revenue rises from 1.22 (2024/25) to 3.89 (2028/29). This measures how many times HRA annual income the outstanding debt represents.
findings.matters: Higher debt multiples reduce headroom for revenue volatility. A ratio of 3.89 means the council's housing rental income must sustain almost 4 years' worth of debt service — a significant concentration risk on one income stream.
findings.quote: Ratio of debt to revenues shows the number of times the level of HRA debt is greater than the HRA gross revenue income. The ratio increases as the HRA debt level is expected to increase in order to deliver new build housing schemes and investment in the existing housing stock.

findings.paper_title: Appendices for Investment Strategies~1
findings.headline: HRA debt growing to 150.6m with interest coverage falling below peer average
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account CFR rises from £71.9m to £150.6m by 2028/29, driven by new-build housing and major stock works. Interest Cover Rate falls from 2.14 to 1.31 over the same period, below the council average of 2.24. Operating surplus will cover interest costs only 1.31 times by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Tight interest coverage signals vulnerability if rental income or housing demand falters, or if interest rates rise. Council is heavily leveraged to sustained HRA rental performance.
findings.quote: The average ICR for councils with an HRA was 2.24 when these indicators were introduced, with councils ranging between 1.20 to 4.50 therefore the Council is estimated to be above the average for 2025/26 but is expected to fall below the average in the future years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates two-year implementation period with significant financial and governance risks
findings.detail: Council is preparing for potential merger with Nottinghamshire authorities into two new unitary councils by April 2028, with shadow elections in 2027. Auditor emphasises need for robust governance, transition cost management, workforce planning, and service continuity over the 2.5-year implementation period while the council retains full sovereignty over its current assets and liabilities.
findings.matters: Major organisational change creates management distraction, increased costs, staff uncertainty, and risk of service disruption; extends financial planning uncertainty through 2028
findings.figures: April 2028 implementation target; final decision expected December summer 2026
findings.quote: Crucially, the Council will need ensure it puts in place robust arrangements to oversee the agreement and implementation of an agreed plan. This includes effective governance and committed leadership, such that there are clear arrangements for decision-making and manage relationships between partners, especially in joint or competing proposals.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan projects structural deficits in 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29
findings.detail: MTFP approved in November 2025 shows General Fund deficit of £228k in 2026/27 with annual deficits projected for the following two years. Council acknowledges need to find further savings and review service provisions, though proposals to mitigate are listed as being developed.
findings.matters: Multi-year deficit projection indicates structural financial imbalance requiring significant savings programme; Fair Funding reforms are explicitly excluded from assumptions so actual position may be worse
findings.figures: £228,000 deficit 2026/27; additional deficits 2027/28 and 2028/29
findings.quote: in November 2025, the OSC was advised on the development of the Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) for 2026/27, informed by current year performance, which projected a deficit on the General Fund revenue budget of £228,000 for 2026/27 with annual deficits in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: General Fund forecast to slip into deficit in Q1 2025/26, despite 2024/25 surplus
findings.detail: While 2024/25 delivered £0.81m surplus (transferred to reserves), Q1 2025/26 forecast shows the General Fund reversing to a deficit position of £0.181m against budget. This signals emerging financial pressure and movement away from the breakeven baseline.
findings.matters: Early-year forecast deficit suggests sustained budget pressure; indicates 2024/25 surplus may have been one-off rather than structural recovery
findings.figures: £0.181m forecast deficit Q1 2025/26 (versus £0.81m surplus in 2024/25)
findings.quote: Our review of the Quarter 1 forecast revenue position, presented to the OSC in August 2025, which indicated that at the end of the financial year, the General Fund is forecast to achieve a deficit position against its budget of £0.181m, which will reduce the level of General Fund balances available.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account reserves depleted by £10.75 million to reduce debt
findings.detail: HRA achieved only a balanced budget position through using significant reserves. £10.75m of HRA reserves were drawn down during the year, primarily a £9.7m transfer to reduce maturing PWLB debt. This reduces HRA's buffer for future demand-led pressures.
findings.matters: Indicates HRA is using reserves to meet current obligations; limits flexibility to absorb cost pressures, void losses, or repair demand spikes without borrowing
findings.figures: £10.75m decrease in HRA reserves; £9.7m transferred to reduce debt
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) reported a balanced position; however, this was achieved through the use of significant reserves, which decreased by £10.75m during the year. The primary driver was a £9.7m transfer from HRA loan reserves to reduce HRA debt in line with Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) loans that matured during the year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision increasing to 9.1%, flagged for continued scrutiny
findings.detail: MRP charge increased from prior year to 9.1% of closing Capital Financing Requirement. While not yet a weakness, auditor flags this as an area requiring continued monitoring, as lower MRP percentages indicate greater reliance on debt repayment through borrowing decisions rather than revenue contributions.
findings.matters: Rising MRP reduces revenue budget flexibility; indicates potential over-reliance on borrowing to fund current operations rather than planned debt repayment
findings.figures: 9.1% of CFR (increased from prior year)
findings.quote: For 2024/25, the Council's general fund MRP is 9.1% of the closing Capital Financing Requirement, which is an increase from the prior year. The lower this percentage, the greater the risk of over-reliance on accounting measures to support the general fund budget, although it does not currently present a risk of significant weakness in arrangements, it is an area for continued scrutiny for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditor not satisfied with Value for Money arrangements; formal finding of significant weaknesses
findings.detail: Auditor's overall conclusion is that arrangements were not in place to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Two significant weaknesses identified: housing repairs procurement and bank reconciliation failures. This is a material audit qualification affecting the council's governance standing.
findings.matters: Formal audit finding on VFM is a regulatory flag; suggests broader control environment concerns beyond the identified issues
findings.figures: Two significant weaknesses identified
findings.quote: We are not satisfied arrangements were in place for the Council to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources, this is because we issued recommendations in relation to significant weaknesses in those arrangements that is relevant to the 2024/25 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Bank reconciliations not performed for seven months across new finance system implementation
findings.detail: Bank reconciliations were not completed between April 2024 and November 2025 following implementation of a new finance system, combined with limited team capacity. Auditor identifies this as a significant weakness: it prevented timely detection of errors or fraud and provided no assurance that the system migration was successful.
findings.matters: Critical financial control failure increases risk of undetected errors in accounts and fraudulent activity; indicates finance team capacity constraints that could affect other controls
findings.figures: 7 months (April 2024 to November 2025)
findings.quote: Through our audit of the financial statements, we identified that bank reconciliations were not performed between April 2024 and November 2025. The Council confirmed that this lapse resulted from the implementation of a new finance system and associated procedural changes, combined with limited team capacity during this period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Audit Completion Report 2024/25
findings.headline: £25 million of housing repairs contracts awarded without proper procurement process
findings.detail: Internal audit investigation into whistleblowing reports found that Housing Repairs Services allocated substantial contract work to external contractors without following the Council's Contract Procedure Rules or approved decision-making process. The Council has since retrospectively approved the full £25 million and implemented corrective action, but this represents a significant governance failure during the year.
findings.matters: Council cannot demonstrate value for money was achieved; creates reputational risk, legal exposure to contract disputes, and loss of credibility with creditors and lenders about internal controls
findings.figures: £25 million
findings.quote: The total value of contracts not procured in accordance with these rules was £25 million. Although the Council has implemented several follow-up actions, detailed below, there remained a lack of appropriate governance during the year, which created a risk of unlawful expenditure and reputational risk.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Savings programme required to address deficits but not detailed in budget proposals
findings.detail: Section 4.4.2 acknowledges 'The Council has a programme of savings that it needs to deliver in order to balance its budget over the medium term and be a sustainable council.' However, the budget report does not detail what these savings are or how they will be achieved. The Head of Paid Service's commentary warns: 'The identified areas of efficiencies and savings will all need to be achieved or if amended alternative realistic and achievable proposals would need to be suggested.'
findings.matters: Absence of savings detail means the council's plan to address structural deficit is not transparent or independently verifiable. This suggests execution risk around the council's ability to meet its financial targets.
findings.figures: £192k (2026/27 deficit to be addressed); growing to £3.587m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The Council has a programme of savings that it needs to deliver in order to balance its budget over the medium term and be a sustainable council.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account capital borrowing of £47m in 2026/27 to fund new build and maintenance
findings.detail: HRA capital programme includes £46.686m prudential borrowing in 2026/27, £24.571m in 2027/28, and £7.492m in 2028/29. HRA interest payable is projected to rise from £4.317m to £7.057m over the three years. The HRA is currently in surplus, but this depends on achieving 4.8% rent increase assumption and maintaining occupancy.
findings.matters: Large HRA borrowing materially increases debt service costs. Slippage in occupancy, rental growth, or management costs would impact ability to service growing debt.
findings.figures: £46,686k HRA borrowing (2026/27); Interest payable £4,317k rising to £7,057k (2028/29)
findings.quote: The HRA capital programme includes £25.331m for the continuation of new council dwellings, to provide additional social housing within the district... Prudential Borrowing 46,686

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: General Fund reserves at £2.125m are essentially at minimum prudent level of £2.1m
findings.detail: At end of 2024/25, General Fund balances stood at £2.125m. The council's own risk assessment determined minimum recommended level to be £2.1m. This leaves minimal buffer above prudent minimum. The S151 Officer flags that reserve adequacy 'will also be determined by the ability to identify the savings from the areas set out as part of the Transformation Strategy and the level of risk associated with the delivery of these.'
findings.matters: Minimal buffer above minimum leaves council with little flexibility to manage unexpected costs or income shortfalls. Drawing reserves below prudent minimums would restrict financial resilience.
findings.figures: £2.125m balances; £2.1m minimum level
findings.quote: At the end of the 2024/25 financial year, General Fund balances stood at £2.125million... the minimum recommended level held in General Fund Balances is £2.1million.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Recruitment difficulties forcing sustained use of agency staff at higher cost
findings.detail: The council faces 'staffing pressures due to recruitment difficulties' with vacant posts across the authority. To maintain service continuity, roles are being filled through agency staff, 'which is more expensive than employing staff directly.' Pay award assumption is 3.2% but remains 'subject to approval by the Local Government Associations.' Actual pay awards could exceed this.
findings.matters: Agency staffing sustains higher cost base. Failure to recruit permanently means ongoing cost inflation. Exceeding pay award assumptions would worsen budget deficit projections.
findings.figures: 3.2% assumed pay award
findings.quote: the Council is also facing staffing pressures due to recruitment difficulties. There are a number of vacant posts throughout the authority, however, in order to ensure that key services continue as expected, some roles have been covered through agency staff, which is more expensive than employing staff directly.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: High proportion of council income from commercial/industrial rents flagged as requiring close monitoring
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges generating 'a high proportion of its income from commercial/industrial rents' and states it 'needs to monitor this income stream closely' because businesses face the same cost pressures (energy, staffing) as the council. Investment Property Income is £2.727m in 2026/27, a material component of funding. No sensitivity analysis is provided for potential rental income decline.
findings.matters: Commercial rental income is exposed to business failure and economic downturn. Material decline in this income could significantly worsen the already-projected General Fund deficits.
findings.figures: £2,727k investment property income (2026/27)
findings.quote: The Council generates a high proportion of its income from commercial/industrial rents. Given that businesses are experiencing the same pressures as the Council, such as increased energy and staffing costs, the council needs to monitor this income stream closely.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Business Rates Pool dissolved due to reset; council loses risk-sharing mechanism
findings.detail: Nottinghamshire Business Rates Pool, operating since 2013/14, is being wound up for 2026/27 onwards. The government's full Business Rates reset will potentially redistribute all previously accumulated growth ('could mean a decrease in retained business rates growth'). The council concluded 'the risks outweigh the rewards in respect of pooling' and will operate standalone. This removes a mechanism for spreading volatility and exposes the council to full individual exposure to revaluations and closure of key employers.
findings.matters: Loss of pooling increases volatility of business rates income and removes ability to share risk across the county. The reset itself poses downside risk to retained growth.
findings.figures: Nottinghamshire member of pool since 2013/14; levy rate was 0% under previous pooling structure
findings.quote: Due to the changes in the system, it is anticipated that the risks outweigh the rewards in respect of pooling. As baseline funding levels have been adjusted to be more accurate, it is more likely that authorities will need a safety net payment... it has therefore been agreed that Nottinghamshire would not operate a Business Rates pool for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: General Fund deficits of £2.862m and £3.587m projected for 2027/28–2028/29 with no identified solutions
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget is balanced via a 2.99% Council Tax increase, but the medium-term plan shows escalating deficits in the following two years. These are approved 'in principle, subject to an annual review' but contain no detailed savings programme or funding proposals to address them. The S151 Officer warns: 'There is an on-going deficit over the medium term at a time where public sector funding becomes tighter' and states the Council 'needs to be prepared to make decisions regarding the services provided, the level at which they are provided.'
findings.matters: Growing out-year deficits indicate the council's service model is unsustainable even with Council Tax rises. Absence of solutions creates material uncertainty about future financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £2,862k (2027/28); £3,587k (2028/29); 2.99% Council Tax increase generates £192k to balance 2026/27
findings.quote: Appendix 1 shows a deficit on the General Fund revenue budget of £192,000 for 2026/27 with annual deficits in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report 1 April 2025 to 30 September 2025
findings.headline: PWLB debt refinancing constrained by expensive early repayment premiums; no debt rescheduling undertaken.
findings.detail: The council holds £50.673m of PWLB borrowing (71% of total debt) where early repayment premiums are expensive. The council has assessed refinancing opportunities and concluded that debt rescheduling is unattractive in the current economic climate. No debt rescheduling activity occurred during the first half of 2025/26, limiting the council's ability to manage or reduce debt costs.
findings.matters: Constrained refinancing options reduce the council's ability to capture savings if interest rates fall; this can lock in higher costs and reduce financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £50.673m PWLB debt of £70.826m total; no debt rescheduling undertaken April-September 2025
findings.quote: The premium charge for early repayment of Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) debt remains relatively expensive for the loans in the Council's portfolio and therefore unattractive for debt rescheduling activity.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report 1 April 2025 to 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Investment returns declining as Bank of England base rates fall; projected income growth now dependent on pessimistic rate forecasts.
findings.detail: Average investment returns have fallen from 5.14% to 4.53% following base rate reductions from 5.25% to 4.00% between July 2024 and August 2025. The council projects base rate will fall further to 3.75% by March 2026. Current projections show investment income exceeding budget by approximately £200k, but this assumption is increasingly at risk if rates decline faster than forecast.
findings.matters: Investment income supports council finances; declining rates reduce future income and budget assumptions are becoming pessimistic, creating risk of shortfall if economic forecasts prove wrong.
findings.figures: Average rate of return decreased from 5.14% to 4.53%; base rate reduced from 5.25% to 4.00%; further reduction to 3.75% expected by March 2026; projected outperformance of £200k to budget
findings.quote: The average rate of return has decreased from 5.14% to 4.53% as a result of the Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee reducing the bank rate from 5.25% to 4.00% from July 2024 to August 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring Report 1 April 2025 to 30 September 2025
findings.headline: Substantial capital borrowing programme: £20m borrowed in first 6 months, with up to £50m more anticipated for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council borrowed £20m in the period April to September 2025 and expects to require up to £50m additional borrowing during 2025/2026. Total borrowing at 30 September 2025 was £70.826m, comprising £50.673m from PWLB, £20m from other local authorities, and £153k from the Racecourse Trust. This represents an increase of £14.5m from 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: The scale and timing of borrowing signals significant capital investment or refinancing needs; understanding future borrowing requirements helps lenders assess debt trajectory and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £20m borrowed April-September 2025; up to £50m more anticipated in 2025/26; total outstanding borrowing £70.826m at 30 September 2025 (increase of £14.5m since 31 March 2025)
findings.quote: During the period 1 April 2025 to 30 September 2025, £20m in new loans were taken out. It is currently anticipated that up to £50m of borrowing will be required during 2025/2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Consistent property income shortfalls across commercial, industrial, and retail portfolios
findings.detail: Commercial Development (£41k shortfall), Industrial Development (£144k shortfall), and Allotments (£12k shortfall) all report lower income than budgeted due to vacant properties. Retail Development also shows lower lettings income.
findings.matters: Multiple property-based income sources underperforming simultaneously suggests either weak local economic conditions or aging/poor-quality assets. Property income is discretionary; if it deteriorates further, the council loses flexibility for debt servicing.
findings.figures: Commercial £41k shortfall, Industrial £144k shortfall, Allotments £12k shortfall
findings.quote: Lower income than expected due to vacant properties

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Legal Services forecasting 31% budget overspend on agency and external legal costs
findings.detail: Legal Services is budgeted at £456k but forecast to reach £600k — a £144k overspend (31%) — driven by "Additional agency costs and external legal expenses compared to budget."
findings.matters: Material unexplained legal cost increases often signal regulatory issues, disputes, or governance problems the council has not disclosed. A 31% overspend in a small budget line warrants scrutiny.
findings.figures: Budget £456k, forecast £600k, variance £144k overspend
findings.quote: Additional agency costs and external legal expenses compared to budget

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Car Parks reversed from £80k income generator to £98k cost, with further income loss expected from capital works
findings.detail: Car Parks Operations moved from a budgeted £80k annual income to a forecast £98k cost — a £178k swing. The variance is attributed to "lower than expected income due to works to Council Car Parks" plus increased building maintenance costs.
findings.matters: A discretionary income source (car parks) turning to cost during major repairs signals either aging infrastructure or capital works with long payback periods. A lender tracking independent revenue streams needs to know when they disappear.
findings.figures: Budget £80k income, forecast £98k cost, variance £178k unfavorable
findings.quote: Increased building maintenance costs and lower than expected income due to works to Council Car Parks

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Structural failure to achieve budgeted vacancy savings across six service areas
findings.detail: Contact Centre, Debtors Recovery, Human Resources, Sheltered Housing, Housing Needs, and Homefinder all report that staffing vacancies assumed in budgets cannot be delivered in practice. The council cannot operate these services at reduced staffing levels.
findings.matters: This indicates vacancies are operationally impossible, not cost targets being missed. If this pattern continues into future years, the council cannot deliver the savings plans needed to close its £277m–£639m funding gap.
findings.figures: Contact Centre £15k, Debtors Recovery £10k, Human Resources £19k, Sheltered Housing £31k, Housing Needs £15k, Homefinder £10k unfavorable variances from unreachable vacancy targets
findings.quote: Budgeted vacancy savings not expected to be achieved

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Housing void levels doubled from budgeted 1.75% to actual 3.88%, costing £926k in lost rental income
findings.detail: The HRA dwelling rents budget assumed 1.75% vacancies but actual void level now stands at 3.88%, generating a £926k unfavorable variance on £30.8m annual rental income. This represents a 2.13% increase in void rates.
findings.matters: HRA income is the council's most stable revenue stream and is relied upon for debt servicing. Rapidly rising voids signal either deteriorating housing stock condition, longer re-letting times, or local housing market weakness.
findings.figures: Budgeted void level 1.75%, actual 3.88%; variance £926k unfavorable on £30,799k budget
findings.quote: Less rental income expected due to higher level of void properties than when the budget was set. The budget was set on a void level of 1.75%, void level currently at 3.88%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Savings gap of £277m for 2026/27 and £639m for 2027/28 remain unidentified
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial plan requires savings of £2.160m for 2026/27 but has only identified £1.848m, leaving a £277m gap. For 2027/28, the target is £2.594m but only £1.920m identified, leaving a £639m gap.
findings.matters: Unidentified savings of this scale in future years represent a fundamental funding problem. If the council cannot find savings plans worth 40%+ of required reductions, it signals structural financial stress ahead.
findings.figures: 2026/27: target £2.160m, identified £1.848m, unidentified £277m; 2027/28: target £2.594m, identified £1.920m, unidentified £639m
findings.quote: Savings still to be identified - 277,083 638,860

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Significant capital budget carry-forward indicates delivery capacity constraints
findings.detail: Across both General Fund and HRA, £34.3 million (34% and 21% respectively) of capital budgets are being carried forward to 2026/27. General Fund forecast spend is only 64% of budget; HRA only 73%. By quarter 2, only 13% of General Fund and 25% of HRA budgets have been spent.
findings.matters: Large carry-forward of capital budgets across the council suggests either procurement delays, delivery planning issues, or constrained capacity to execute planned investment, which extends timelines and defers benefits.
findings.figures: General Fund: Budget £54.4m, Q2 actual £7.1m (13%), forecast £34.9m (64% of budget), carry forward £18.75m (34%); HRA: Budget £73.4m, Q2 actual £18.3m (25%), forecast £53.9m (73%), carry forward £15.56m (21%)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Council-owned property works program significantly underspent with £8 million carried forward
findings.detail: The £10.7 million property maintenance and improvements program is only forecast to spend £2.6 million in 2025/26, with £8.1 million (76% of budget) carried forward to next year, indicating the program is progressing significantly slower than planned.
findings.matters: Significant slippage in property maintenance suggests either capacity constraints in managing the estate or changed delivery priorities, affecting asset condition management across the council's property portfolio.
findings.figures: Budget £10.7 million; forecast full year £2.6 million; carry forward £8.09 million
findings.quote: Project on going

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: CRP Streetscaping project delayed pending planning agreement and final contract price
findings.detail: The £2 million CRP Streetscaping public realm project is underway but delayed due to design changes required to address planning considerations. Majority spend is now forecast for 2026/27, with final contract price not yet agreed (expected January 2026).
findings.matters: Planning-driven delays and pending contract price agreement on a regeneration project create execution risk and extend delivery, affecting both budget certainty and project outcomes.
findings.figures: Budget £1.985 million; forecast £596k; carry forward £1.39 million
findings.quote: Project underway but delayed with design to account for planning considerations. Majority spend within 2026/27, subject to final contract price being agreed expected January 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Mansfield Connect major regeneration project extended into 2026/27 with soft strip work ongoing
findings.detail: The £8.7 million Mansfield Connect project has been split into multiple contracts. Asbestos removal and bridge removal on schedule for completion by 2025/26 year end, but primary PCSA 2 construction work is now scheduled into 2026/27, with £2.4 million carried forward.
findings.matters: A major town center regeneration project experiencing phased delivery affects economic development timeline and capital cash flow planning over multiple years.
findings.figures: Total budget £8.7 million; forecast full year £6.3 million; carry forward £2.4 million
findings.quote: PCSA 2 instruction issued to Kier, alongside separate contract for soft strip, asbestos removal and bridge removal. The latter to be completed by 2025/26 year end. The former into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Major capital programs not yet commenced despite significant budgets allocated
findings.detail: Crematorium Refurbishment (£961k) and Food Waste Collection (£852k) programmes have not started and are being carried forward entirely to 2026/27 with no spend by quarter 2. Both programmes show no progress on delivery.
findings.matters: Capital budgets allocated but not deployed suggest either planning delays, procurement challenges, or delivery readiness issues that extend investment timelines and defer service benefits.
findings.figures: Crematorium budget £961,691 with £861,691 carried forward; Food Waste Collection budget £852,260 with £852,260 carried forward; both have zero spend at Q2
findings.quote: Construction expected to commence in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Walkden Street Car Park requires demolition following structural collapse
findings.detail: A car park building collapse is triggering reactive demolition works scheduled to begin October 2025. This represents an unplanned major structural maintenance issue requiring capital expenditure, though the budget allocation (£700,000 forecast vs £100,000 budgeted) suggests the scale was initially underestimated.
findings.matters: Asset failure requiring urgent demolition indicates potential backlog of infrastructure maintenance and reactive capital demands, which affects budget planning and operational continuity.
findings.figures: Budget £100,000; forecast £700,000; variance +£600,000 overspend
findings.quote: Following collapse building to be demolished October 2025 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Berry Hill Quarry cliff stabilization project being delivered in phases with significant delay
findings.detail: The £3.3 million project is being re-profiled from delivery this year. Section 1 will commence in January 2026 with completion March 2026, with remaining sections in 2026/27. This represents a major infrastructure project being phased over two years rather than completed as originally planned, with £2.59 million carried forward.
findings.matters: A major capital project delay indicates delivery capacity constraints and suggests infrastructure investment is extending beyond planned timelines, affecting both budget profiles and asset completion.
findings.figures: Budget £3.27 million; forecast full-year spend £678,000; carry forward £2.59 million
findings.quote: The project is now having to be delivered in sections. Section 1 is to be commissioned in January 2026 with a completion of March 2026. The remaining section will be commissioned over the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Prior-year savings proposals remain undelivered and the council holds £500k reserve against non-delivery risk
findings.detail: The risk assessment table identifies '2025/26 savings identified that the Council is unable to implement' as a medium-risk item with a £500k reserve held against non-delivery. If the council cannot deliver savings already identified for 2025/26, this undermines confidence in its ability to deliver the £2.6m–£3.4m of unidentified savings required for 2027/28–2028/29.
findings.matters: A track record of undelivered savings proposals suggests the council may struggle to address its emerging deficits, creating risk that deficits will widen or be covered by reserve drawdown rather than sustainable action.
findings.figures: £500k reserve held against 2025/26 savings non-delivery; £2.597m and £3.362m unidentified deficits in 2027/28 and 2028/29
findings.quote: 2025/26 savings identified that the Council is unable to implement

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: HRA debt service costs rising sharply despite current surplus, reducing future investment capacity
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme totals £50.9m in 2026/27, of which £40.9m is funded by prudential borrowing. HRA interest payable rises from £4.54m (2026/27) to £7.141m (2028/29), an increase of 57% over three years. While the HRA is currently in surplus, rising debt service costs will increasingly consume available revenue and constrain capacity to invest in further new social housing (the business plan allows no new social housing beyond April 2028).
findings.matters: Rapidly rising debt service costs reduce financial flexibility and create vulnerability if interest rates remain elevated or if rental income falls due to void rates or rent arrears.
findings.figures: HRA capital programme £50.872m (2026/27), funded by £40.901m prudential borrowing; interest payable £4.54m (2026/27) rising to £7.141m (2028/29); no new social housing planned beyond April 2028
findings.quote: The HRA capital programme includes £21.486m for the continuation of new council dwellings, to provide additional social housing within the district. The current business plan does not allow for any new social and affordable housing beyond April 2028.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review assumptions are uncertain and could further reduce government funding below current budget estimates
findings.detail: The budget is based on 'initial estimates of the potential impact of the Fair Funding Review' with the council acknowledging it 'will continue to monitor announcements from Central Government in order to update the final budget position'. Several grants (New Homes Bonus, Funding Guarantee, Domestic Abuse Prevention Grant, Homelessness Prevention Grant) are being 'rolled in' to Revenue Support Grant, but the distribution mechanism and actual amounts are not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: Government funding changes could reduce council income below current assumptions, worsening deficits that the council has already failed to identify solutions for in years 2 and 3 of this plan.
findings.figures: Government grants assumed at £4.49m per annum; specific impact of Fair Funding Review not quantified
findings.quote: The Council has based the draft budget figures on initial estimates of the potential impact of the Fair Funding Review, and will continue to monitor announcements from Central Government in order to update the final budget position.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Council is heavily exposed to commercial property income in economically stressed market
findings.detail: Mansfield District Council generates a 'high proportion of its income from commercial/industrial rents', with investment property income budgeted at £2.771m (2026/27), falling to £2.652m (2028/29). The council itself flags that 'businesses are experiencing the same pressures as the Council, such as increased energy and staffing costs', and requires 'close monitoring' of this income stream. Loss or reduction of commercial rents would directly worsen the council's deficit position.
findings.matters: If commercial tenants default, leave, or negotiate reduced rents due to economic pressure, this multi-million pound income stream could decline precisely when the council is already facing structural deficits.
findings.quote: The Council generates a high proportion of its income from commercial/industrial rents. Given that businesses are experiencing the same pressures as the Council, such as increased energy and staffing costs, the council needs to monitor this income stream closely.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: Full business rates reset in 2026/27 threatens accumulated growth and creates income volatility at critical time
findings.detail: The council faces a full reset of the Business Rates system in 2026/27 in which 'all growth accumulated to date is potentially subject to redistribution across the sector'. The document acknowledges this 'could mean a decrease in retained business rates growth at the start of the reset period', but does not quantify the potential loss. Retained business rates are budgeted at £5.07m annually, and loss of accumulated growth would immediately worsen the council's deficit position.
findings.matters: Unquantified loss of business rates growth income would compound the council's existing deficit problems at the exact point when the budget already shows structural imbalance for 2027/28 onwards.
findings.figures: Retained business rates £5.07m per annum; full reset scheduled 2026/27; loss of accumulated growth amount not quantified
findings.quote: Under a full reset, all growth accumulated to date is potentially subject to redistribution across the sector for the forthcoming reset period. This could mean a decrease in retained business rates growth at the start of the reset period.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.headline: General Fund faces growing deficits of £3m+ from 2027/28 onwards with no identified solutions proposed
findings.detail: The budget shows a £228k deficit in 2026/27 covered by council tax and fees increases, but unresolved deficits of £3.015m in 2027/28 and £3.970m in 2028/29. Appendix 2 shows proposed solutions (council tax rises of £380-570k and fees rises of £38k) would eliminate only £418-608k of these deficits, leaving structural gaps of £2.597m and £3.362m unaddressed. The S151 Officer notes the council faces deficits 'at a time where public sector funding becomes tighter' and must prepare 'to make decisions regarding the services provided'.
findings.matters: Unidentified solutions to multi-million pound deficits signal the council will need to make substantial service reductions or find additional revenue sources, reducing financial stability and refinancing certainty for lenders.
findings.figures: £3.015m deficit 2027/28, £3.970m deficit 2028/29; proposed solutions cover only £418k and £608k respectively
findings.quote: There is an on-going deficit over the medium term at a time where public sector funding becomes tighter. The Council needs to be prepared to make decisions regarding the services provided, the level at which they are provided and the way in which they are provided if it is to maintain balanced and sustainable budgets for the future

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Q2 Performance Data 2025-26
findings.headline: Non-emergency housing repairs are underperforming at 80.97% completion against an 83.10% target, with 417 contractor repairs overdue
findings.detail: Non-emergency repairs are completing below target, with 417 contractor repairs overdue at period end and 36 DLO repairs overdue. The council has initiated an intervention plan but the backlog persists.
findings.matters: A large overdue repair backlog, especially from external contractors, indicates resource or capacity constraints in the housing management function and could escalate into higher costs or tenant complaints.
findings.figures: 80.97% completion vs 83.10% target; 417 contractor repairs overdue; 36 DLO repairs overdue
findings.quote: Proportion of non-emergency responsive repairs completed within the landlord's target timescale. 80.97% 83.10% ⯃ é

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Q2 Performance Data 2025-26
findings.headline: Gas safety compliance requires legal intervention to access properties after repeated refusals
findings.detail: Gas safety compliance is at 99.72% against a 100% target. The council has implemented a formal legal process after two prior letters to non-cooperative property holders, now issuing pre-legal letters to compel access for required safety checks.
findings.matters: Inability to access rental properties for safety compliance has escalated to legal intervention, indicating a subset of tenants are resisting routine inspections. This is a control and asset management risk.
findings.figures: 99.72% compliant vs 100% target; legal process adopted with pre-legal letters after 2 no-access letters
findings.quote: Gas fluctuates between 100% and 99% due to no access. the no access process is in place and legal process has been adopted with pre legal letters now sent after 2 no access letters.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Q2 Performance Data 2025-26
findings.headline: Rental income is being lost at 3.41% of rent through vacant dwellings against a 1.75% target
findings.detail: The council's void loss rate is nearly double the target, driven by extended relet times. Across all relet types, properties are staying vacant significantly longer than targets—195 days average versus an 80-day target for all relets, with major works taking 204 days against a 95-day target.
findings.matters: Void losses directly reduce rental income. At this rate of loss, the council is foregoing material revenue that would otherwise service debt or be available for services.
findings.figures: 3.41% void loss vs 1.75% target; average relet 195 days vs 80 days target; major works relets 204 days vs 95 days target
findings.quote: % of rent lost through vacant dwellings (all voids, including major works) 3.41% 1.75% X é

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Q2 Performance Data 2025-26
findings.headline: Electrical safety compliance is 95.24% with a new contractor mobilizing October 2025 to close the gap
findings.detail: The council is significantly below the 100% target for required electrical assessments in housing. A new five-year contract with supplier Dodds is mobilizing in October 2025, with properties targeted for full compliance by Christmas 2025 for C1/C2 risk categories and end of March 2026 for C3.
findings.matters: Persistent non-compliance with electrical safety standards exposes the council to legal liability and tenant safety risk. A new contractor dependency and extended compliance timeline is material to asset quality and operational risk.
findings.figures: 95.24% compliant vs 100% target; C1/C2 completion target Christmas 2025, C3 by end March 2026
findings.quote: The company Dodds have been awarded the 5 year contract as the sole supplier of EICR due to mobilise in October 2025. All properties targeted for compliance by Xmas, with all C1 and C2 completed and all C3 by the end of March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating structural uncertainty with tight implementation deadline
findings.detail: Mansfield is working with other Nottinghamshire councils on a government-mandated reorganisation (Option 1e: north-south split). Two fixed-term posts funded from reserves manage this. The business case goes to Full Council 25 November for submission to government by 28 November 2025. Restructuring of this scale typically creates cost pressures, service disruption, and leadership distraction.
findings.matters: Major structural reorganisation under tight government deadline creates execution risk, hidden costs, and period of governance uncertainty that affects credit quality.
findings.figures: Two fixed-term posts funded from reserves; 28 November deadline
findings.quote: Mansfield District Council has worked with other Nottinghamshire councils throughout 2025/26 to prepare the business case for the Council's preferred option, known as Option 1e, which is based on a north-south split within the County. This option will be presented to Full Council on 25th November, in time for submission to government by their deadline of 28th November 2025.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: Council relies heavily on commercial/industrial rents but tenants are under the same economic pressures
findings.detail: Mansfield generates a disproportionate share of income from commercial and industrial property rents. The council explicitly flags that its tenants face rising energy and staffing costs, forcing it to actively monitor this income stream. No material income shortfall is yet showing, but the risk is live.
findings.matters: Commercial income concentration creates revenue volatility; tenant distress often precedes rent arrears and covenant breaches.
findings.figures: Proportion not quantified in this extract
findings.quote: The council generates a high proportion of its income from commercial/industrial rents. Given that business are experiencing the same pressures as Mansfield District Council, such as increased energy and staffing costs, the council needs to continue to monitor this income stream closely.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 2
findings.headline: General Fund balances will fall £0.55m below the council's own minimum threshold
findings.detail: The council forecasts General Fund balances of £2.045m at year-end, which is £0.55m below the minimum level it approved during budget setting. This will require a transfer from earmarked reserves to restore the position, reducing flexibility for future shocks.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits a council's ability to manage unexpected costs and signals tightening financial headroom to lenders.
findings.figures: £2.045m forecasted balance; £0.55m shortfall; planned transfer from earmarked reserves
findings.quote: It is forecasted that by the 31 March 2026, General Fund balances will stand at £2.045m, which is £0.55m below the minimum level of balances the Council approved as part of the budget setting process.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecast to run £0.852m deficit despite being set as a balanced budget
findings.detail: The HRA was approved as a balanced budget with all expenditure to be covered by dwelling rents and other housing-related fees. Q1 forecast shows an £0.852m deficit, with dwelling rents £926k below budget at £29.814m against budgeted £30.740m, indicating collection or affordability pressures.
findings.matters: Persistent HRA deficits require reserve drawdown and indicate the council cannot sustain its landlord function at current service levels and pricing, raising questions about future viability of council housing and need for rent increases.
findings.figures: £0.852m forecast deficit; dwelling rents £926k shortfall (£29.814m vs £30.740m budget)
findings.quote: Table 3 shows the year end position as at 31 st March 2026 for the Housing Revenue Account which is a deficit position of £0.852m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: General Fund balances forecast to fall £0.156m below the council's approved minimum reserve level
findings.detail: At Q1 forecast, General Fund balances are estimated at £1.944m by 31 March 2026, falling short of the minimum level the council approved in its budget setting process. The council plans to address this shortfall by transferring from earmarked reserves in the final accounts process, but the core position is below target.
findings.matters: Falling below minimum reserves signals weaker financial resilience and can affect borrowing capacity and credit risk assessment, particularly if this trend continues in future years.
findings.figures: £1.944m forecast balance; £0.156m below approved minimum
findings.quote: It is forecasted that by the 31 March 2026, General Fund balances will stand at £1.944m, which is £0.156m below the minimum level of balances the Council approved as part of the budget setting process.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Food Waste Collection vehicle delivery delayed to early 2027 affecting service implementation
findings.detail: Food Waste Collection has a £852k budget in 2025/26 but vehicles are ordered with 'delivery and payment early 2027', meaning the capital spend and service launch will not happen in the planned financial year. This is a material delay to a waste service change.
findings.matters: Service implementation delays create financial strain (budget allocated but not spent) and may indicate procurement bottlenecks or supply chain issues. The council will need to finance or carry forward this budget.
findings.figures: £852,260 capital budget; delivery early 2027
findings.quote: Food Waste Collection 852,260 -852,260 852,260 0 0 0 Food Waste vehicles ordered with delivery and payment early 2027

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Multiple capital projects carried forward £1.42m to 2026/27 indicating slippage
findings.detail: Five schemes are being carried forward from 2025/26 to 2026/27 including Walkden St Car Park (£250k), Four Seasons Car Park (£979k), civic centre door replacement (£30k), asset surveys (£20k), and theatre museum atrium work (£145k). Four Seasons is noted as 'scheme to continue' rather than complete.
findings.matters: Project slippage ties up budgets, creates cash flow unpredictability, and may indicate procurement delays, planning issues, or underestimated delivery timescales. The large car park projects (£1.2m combined) suggest either scope changes or delayed supply chains.
findings.figures: £1,423,983 total carry-forward
findings.quote: Walkden St Car Park Works 249,817 Scheme to continue in to 2026/27; Four Seasons Car Park Works 979,166 Scheme to continue in to 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Large HRA new build and refurbishment schemes showing delivery concentration risk
findings.detail: Three major housing schemes (Centenary Road £18.1m, Community Heart £4.1m, Town Centre Development £7.3m totalling £29.5m) have spent only £1.4m in Q1 but forecast full-year spending. The Community Heart project is stated to complete this financial year despite only 16% spend by Q1, with retention to be paid in the following year.
findings.matters: Concentration of major spend in later quarters creates cash flow timing risk and execution risk. If any project slips, the council may miss its capital forecast; if all deliver on time, there will be a sharp Q2-Q4 spending profile. Retention payments due next year also extend the cash impact.
findings.figures: Centenary Road Phase 3: £18,127,752 budget; Community Heart: £4,084,092 (retention 12 months after completion)
findings.quote: Community Heart Bellamy Rd 4,084,092 666,799 -3,417,293 4,084,092 0 0 0 Project to be completd in this financial year. Retention to be paid 12 months after practical completion

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Disabled adaptations budget overspent and requesting £400k additional funding
findings.detail: Disabled Adaptations was budgeted at £1.1m but only £302k was spent in Q1 with a note stating the budget will be spent and a virement is being requested to increase it by £400k (36% increase). The original budget appears to have underestimated both volume and unit costs.
findings.matters: For social landlords, disabled adaptations are both a statutory duty and demand-driven. An underestimated budget suggests either demographic shift in the tenant population (aging stock) or a backlog being addressed, either of which affects ongoing capital requirements.
findings.figures: £1,100,000 budget; £400,000 virement requested
findings.quote: Disabled Adaptations 1,100,000 301,826 -798,174 1,100,000 0 0 0 High number of referrals received, budget will be spent. Virement requested to increase budget

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Unbudgeted damp and mould remediation work in housing stock requiring £1.01m virement
findings.detail: The council budgeted £2.03m for Section 11 and Damp/Mould work but is requesting a virement of £1.017m to fund discovered work, nearly doubling the original allocation. This suggests the condition survey identified significantly more remedial work than initially anticipated.
findings.matters: Housing stock deterioration discovered mid-year is a sign of deferred maintenance backlog and erodes the council's HRA viability assumptions. The fact that work was being discovered rather than planned suggests either poor asset condition tracking or that the council is now addressing previously tolerated defects.
findings.figures: £2,034,000 original budget; £1,017,000 virement requested
findings.quote: Section 11 and Damp/Mould 1,017,000 High levels of works being identified

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Staffing cost inflation: agency costs and planned vacancy savings not materialising
findings.detail: Agency costs mentioned for Council Tax Collection, Legal Services, Development Management, and Design Services. Separately, multiple service areas report 'Budgeted vacancy savings not expected to be achieved' (HR, Sheltered Housing, Cemeteries). Dog Control Service facing cost increase from new contract. These combine to suggest staffing inflation outpacing planned savings.
findings.matters: If a council cannot deliver budgeted vacancy savings and is paying more for agency cover, it has less financial headroom than the budget assumed. This is structural cost pressure.
findings.figures: Legal Services variance £33k; Dog Control Service variance £16k; multiple departments citing unachieved vacancy savings
findings.quote: Budgeted vacancy savings not expected to be achieved

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Income streams under pressure from property vacancies and weak demand
findings.detail: Commercial Development revenue down from lower income due to vacant properties; Industrial Development down from lower rental income due to vacancies. Garden Waste Collection also reporting less income than budgeted. These are demand/utilisation issues, not one-off factors.
findings.matters: Multiple revenue sources squeezed simultaneously suggests underlying economic weakness in the council's area or loss of competitive position for its commercial assets.
findings.figures: Commercial Development variance £43k; Industrial Development variance £116k; Garden Waste variance £43k
findings.quote: Commercial Development – Lower income than expected due to vacant properties

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Savings plans failing to deliver: £279m shortfall emerging for 26/27, £641m for 27/28
findings.detail: The Savings Tracker shows the council has already identified £1.74m of its £1.82m target for 25/26 (£136k shortfall), but faces gaps of £279m in 26/27 and £641m in 27/28. Across all departments, 'Establishment savings not yet met' appears repeatedly (Sheltered Housing, Cemeteries, Human Resources). The Corporate savings line alone shows £249m shortfall each year.
findings.matters: A council with growing unidentified savings gaps has no solution to future budget pressures and faces real risk of mid-year cuts or service withdrawal. Lenders assess whether a council can fund its debt from revenue.
findings.figures: 25/26 shortfall £135,597k; 26/27 savings still to identify £279,083k; 27/28 £640,860k
findings.quote: Savings still to be identified - 279,083 640,860

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Revenue and Capital Forecast Year-End Position, at Quarter 1
findings.headline: Housing void rate doubled to 3.43%, eroding rental income by £926k
findings.detail: The budget assumed void rental properties would remain at 1.75% of stock. Q1 actual is running at 3.43%. This creates a £926k variance against a £30.8m annual rental income target. For a housing-dependent council, the doubling of void rate signals management or demand problems.
findings.matters: Lost housing rental income weakens General Fund cash flow and indicates underlying issues with housing quality, demand, or management that affect the council's revenue base.
findings.figures: Dwelling Rents: budgeted 1.75% void, actual 3.43% void; variance £926k against £30,799k annual rent budget
findings.quote: The budget was set on a void level of 1.75%, void level currently at 3.43%.

news_drafts.lead: Lenders assess long-term HRA sustainability and financing assumptions; if this pattern continues, the HRA will face pressure to borrow at scale or raise rents significantly to fund capital needs, both carrying financial and political risk.

news_drafts.lead: Reserve adequacy is a key resilience indicator; balances at or near minimum level mean the council has little flexibility to absorb unexpected costs, income shortfalls, or emergencies without cutting services or seeking new borrowing.
